drafts.title: I cloned my own voice for $47 and called my dad. He didn't know it wasn't me. Here are the 12 signals that reveal AI-generated voices.
drafts.content:
Spent a weekend testing 5 voice cloning platforms (ElevenLabs, Resemble AI, OpenAI TTS-HD, Play.ht, Lovo) using three samples of my own voice. Then called my dad with each one.

He couldn't tell which call was the clone.

This isn't a theoretical security risk anymore. The FTC reported $25M+ in voice cloning fraud losses in 2025, up 3x from 2023. The scam script is almost always the same: your kid/grandkid is in trouble, needs money, please don't tell anyone.

The interesting part is that AI voices DO leave forensic traces — just not ones your ear reliably catches. I've been building a browser-based detector that runs 12 spectral and prosodic signals on any uploaded clip:

- High-frequency rolloff slope (AI vocoders smooth this too much)
- Background floor variance (AI voices are unnaturally quiet in the pauses)
- Breath event frequency (most AI voices have near-zero breath events)
- F0 jitter and shimmer (real voices have micro-variation AI removes)
- Lip click presence (biological artifact that's almost never in synthetic audio)
- ...and 7 more

All runs offline in the browser. Audio never leaves your device.

Wrote up the full methodology, my test results on all 5 platforms, and what to listen for in real-time if you're on a suspicious call:

https://tinytools-smoky.vercel.app/voice-cloning-detector/blog/i-cloned-my-voice-sent-it-to-my-dad-he-picked-up-heres-how-to-catch-ai-voice-scams-2026/

drafts.title: Adobe Stock is rejecting AI images without C2PA manifests — most AI creators have never generated one
drafts.content:
Discovered this the annoying way: Adobe Stock started bouncing AI-generated image submissions earlier this year. After some digging, the issue was missing C2PA provenance metadata — a JSON manifest embedded in the file that declares what created it.

The Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) is backed by Adobe, Microsoft, Google, BBC, Intel, Sony, OpenAI, and roughly 2,000 others. It's the technical standard for declaring whether content is AI-generated. Adobe Stock reads it automatically. LinkedIn started surfacing it in 'About this image' popups. EU AI Act enforcement for synthetic media disclosure hits fully in August 2026.

The problem: if you're generating images with Midjourney, local Stable Diffusion, or anything outside Firefly's web app, you're getting zero C2PA metadata by default. The tooling to add it yourself used to require running a Rust CLI (c2patool) with a JSON config file.

Built a browser-based version of this. Upload your image, fill in 3 fields (creator name, generative tool, training data assertion), download the manifest-embedded version. Runs offline, image never leaves your device.

drafts.content:
Built a browser-based C2PA manifest generator after watching Adobe Stock reject AI-generated image submissions for missing provenance metadata.

C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) is the technical standard backed by Adobe, Microsoft, Google, BBC, Intel, Sony, OpenAI et al. for declaring how content was created. It embeds a signed JSON manifest into the image file. Adobe Stock reads it. LinkedIn surfaces it. EU AI Act Article 50 mandates synthetic media disclosure with full enforcement in August 2026.

If you're generating images outside of Adobe Firefly's web app — Midjourney downloads, local SD, ComfyUI — you get no C2PA metadata by default. The official tooling is c2patool (Rust CLI + JSON config), which is fine for engineers and useless for everyone else.

This runs entirely in the browser, no server-side processing. Fill in creator name, generative tool, and training data assertion (not_allowed / constrained / allowed). Cryptographic signing is handled in-browser via the C2PA JS SDK.
